title: Modular arithmetic
lead: Clock arithmetic is the language of nearly every cipher.
sections: The idea

Modular arithmetic keeps only the remainder after division. On a 12-hour clock, 9 + 5 is 2, because 14 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 12. We write 14 ≡ 2 (mod 12). Ciphers use it so letters wrap around the alphabet instead of running off the end.
Letters as numbers
Number A = 0 up to Z = 25. A Caesar shift by k is then C = (P + k) mod 26.
Inverses
To undo multiplication by a, we need a number a⁻¹ with a × a⁻¹ ≡ 1. That exists only when a shares no factor with the modulus. This is why an affine cipher allows only 12 multipliers mod 26.
example: Find the inverse of 5 mod 26
Try 5 × 21 = 105 = 4 × 26 + 1. So 5 × 21 ≡ 1, and the inverse of 5 is 21. To decrypt an affine cipher with a = 5, multiply by 21. With 12 multipliers and 26 shifts, the affine cipher has 312 keys.

title: Counting keys
lead: Key count tells you what brute force costs. It says little about real security.
sections: Permutations
A substitution alphabet is a rearrangement of 26 letters. There are 26 choices for A, 25 for B, and so on: 26! in total.
Bits
Keys are compared in bits: the base-2 logarithm of the count. Each extra bit doubles the search.
Why it is not enough
Simple substitution has about 88 bits of key, more than DES, yet a page of it falls in moments to frequency analysis. A large keyspace is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.
example: How big is the Enigma's keyspace?

Choosing 3 rotors in order from 5 gives 60 arrangements. Start positions give 26³ = 17,576. Ten plugboard pairs give 150,738,274,937,250 wirings. Multiplying gives about 1.59 × 10²⁰ settings, around 67 bits, before counting ring settings.

title: Frequency and chi-squared
lead: Languages have fingerprints, and a substitution cannot erase them.
sections: Letter statistics
In English, E makes up roughly 12.7% of letters, and Z well under 0.1%. A substitution relabels letters but keeps those rates.
Measuring fit
Chi-squared compares the counts we see, O, with those expected, E: the sum over letters of (O − E)² ÷ E. Smaller means a better fit. For a Caesar cipher, try all shifts and keep the smallest.
example: A small chi-squared calculation
Suppose a 100-letter text has 11 Es where 12.7 are expected. That letter contributes (11 − 12.7)² ÷ 12.7 ≈ 0.23. Adding such terms over all 26 letters gives the score.

title: Index of coincidence
lead: One number reveals whether a text is built from one alphabet or many.
sections: Definition
Pick two letters from a text at random. The index of coincidence, IC, is the chance that they match: the sum over letters of n(n − 1), divided by N(N − 1).
Why it works

For a language, IC is approximately the sum of each letter's probability squared, about 0.066 in English. For uniform random letters it is 26 × (1/26)², which is 1/26 ≈ 0.0385. Any simple substitution leaves IC unchanged, because it only renames letters.
Finding key length
Take every Lth letter. If L is the key length, those letters share one shift, so their IC rises towards 0.066.
example: IC of AABB
There are N = 4 letters, with counts 2 and 2. IC = (2×1 + 2×1) ÷ (4×3) = 4/12 ≈ 0.333.

title: Entropy and unicity distance
lead: How much ciphertext do you need before only one answer makes sense?
sections: Entropy
Claude Shannon measured information in bits. A source with probabilities p has entropy H = −Σ p log₂ p. Twenty-six equally likely letters give log₂ 26 ≈ 4.7 bits per letter.
Redundancy
English carries only about 1.5 bits per letter once its patterns are taken into account. The difference, roughly 3.2 bits, is redundancy, and redundancy is what codebreakers exploit.
Unicity distance
Shannon's estimate of the ciphertext needed to pin down a unique key is U = H(K) ÷ D, the key entropy divided by the redundancy per letter.
example: Simple substitution

H(K) = log₂ 26! ≈ 88.4 bits and D ≈ 3.2 bits. So U ≈ 27.6, or about 28 letters. Below that, several readings can look equally good. This is why the 44-letter Tamam Shud code resists any confident answer once a stronger system is allowed.

title: Scoring text: log-likelihood
lead: How a computer judges whether a guess looks like language.
sections: N-grams
Count how often each run of four letters appears in a large body of text. That estimates the probability of each quadgram.
Add logs, not probabilities
Multiplying thousands of tiny probabilities overflows a computer's range. Logarithms turn products into sums, so a text's score is the sum of log-probabilities.
A warning
A high score is not proof. When the solver has freedom to choose many symbols, it can produce text that scores well and means nothing. This app therefore compares each result with scrambled controls.
example: Comparing two quadgrams
If TION has probability 0.003 and QZXJ has 0.0000001, their log₁₀ values are about −2.52 and −7. The difference of about 4.5 means TION is about 30,000 times more likely.

title: Simulated annealing
lead: A search that sometimes takes a step backwards on purpose.
sections: Hill climbing
Change the key slightly and keep the change if the score improves. It is simple but often gets stuck on a small peak.
Metropolis rule
Accept a worse move with probability e^(Δ/T), where Δ is the score change and T is the temperature. High T allows big jumps, and low T settles down.
Cooling
Start hot and cool slowly. It is modelled on annealing metal, and it is the workhorse of modern classical-cipher solvers.
example: Accepting a bad move
With Δ = −2: at T = 5 the chance is e^(−0.4) ≈ 67%, and at T = 1 it is e^(−2) ≈ 13.5%. Bad moves become rare as the temperature falls.

title: Linear algebra and the Hill cipher
lead: Matrix multiplication scrambles blocks of letters, but linearity is a weakness.
sections: Encryption
Write letters as a vector and multiply by a key matrix mod 26. Each output letter depends on the whole block.
Decryption
You need the inverse matrix mod 26, which exists only if the determinant has no factor in common with 26.
The weakness
Because the system is linear, n known plaintext blocks give n equations, and solving them gives the key.
example: Multiplying gives (3×7 + 3×4, 2×7 + 5×4) = (33, 34) ≡ (7, 8), which is HI. The determinant is 3×5 − 3×2 = 9, whose inverse mod 26 is 3. The inverse matrix is 3 × [[5,−3],[−2,3]] ≡ [[15,17],[20,9]]. Applying that to (7,8) returns (7,4). There are 157,248 invertible 2×2 matrices mod 26.

title: Group theory: Enigma and the cube
lead: Rejewski broke Enigma with permutation theory. The same mathematics runs a Rubik's cube.
sections: Permutations compose
Doing one rearrangement after another is itself a rearrangement. Such a collection is a group: it has an identity and every element can be undone.
Enigma

Each keypress applies a permutation made of the rotors, conjugated around a reflector: E = P⁻¹ R P. Since R swaps letters in pairs with no fixed points, E does too. That is exactly why no letter can encrypt to itself.
Rejewski's insight
Pairing the first and fourth letters of doubled message keys gave permutations whose cycle structure did not depend on the plugboard. That reduced the search to something his team could catalogue.
The cube
Each face turn permutes the 54 stickers. The cube's group has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 elements, and its diameter, the worst-case distance from solved, is 20.
example: An order calculation

R turned four times returns the cube to where it began, so R has order 4. Repeating the sequence (R U) returns to solved after 105 repeats, because its permutation has cycles whose lengths have a least common multiple of 105.

title: Euclid, Euler and RSA
lead: Public-key cryptography rests on an ancient algorithm and an 18th-century theorem.
sections: Greatest common divisor
Euclid's algorithm repeatedly replaces a pair with the smaller number and the remainder. Run backwards, it finds modular inverses.
Euler's theorem
If a and n share no factor, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ(n) counts the numbers below n coprime to it. For n = pq, φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
RSA
Pick e and find d with ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). Then (mᵉ)ᵈ ≡ m. Publishing n and e is safe as long as nobody can factor n to get φ(n).
example: Toy RSA

Take p = 61 and q = 53, so n = 3233 and φ(n) = 3120. With e = 17, the inverse is d = 2753. The message 65 encrypts to 65¹⁷ mod 3233 = 2790, and 2790²⁷⁵³ mod 3233 returns 65. Euclid's method on 1071 and 462: 1071 = 2×462 + 147, 462 = 3×147 + 21, 147 = 7×21, so the gcd is 21.

title: Discrete logarithms
lead: Easy forwards, hard backwards: the engine of key exchange.
sections: The problem
Given g, p and h = gˣ mod p, find x. Computing h is fast by repeated squaring, while reversing it appears hard for large p.
Diffie-Hellman
Alice publishes gᵃ and Bob publishes gᵇ. Each raises the other's value to their secret, reaching gᵃᵇ.
Baby-step giant-step
Writing x = im + j trades memory for time and needs about √p steps. A 31-bit group takes about 46,000 steps instead of two billion.
example: With a = 6, A = 5⁶ mod 23 = 8. With b = 15, B = 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19. Alice computes 19⁶ mod 23 = 2, and Bob computes 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2. They share the secret 2.

title: Finite fields and AES
lead: AES does its arithmetic on bytes in a field with 256 elements.
sections: GF(2⁸)
Treat a byte as a polynomial with bits as coefficients. Addition is XOR. Multiplication is polynomial multiplication reduced by x⁸ + x⁴ + x³ + x + 1.
Why it matters
Every non-zero byte has an inverse, so the arithmetic is reversible. SubBytes is built from those inverses, which makes it highly non-linear.
Confusion and diffusion
SubBytes supplies confusion, and ShiftRows and MixColumns supply diffusion. After a couple of rounds every output byte depends on every input byte.
example: A multiplication from the AES standard
In GF(2⁸), the bytes 0x57 and 0x83 multiply to 0xC1.

title: The birthday bound
lead: Collisions arrive far sooner than intuition suggests.
sections: The surprise
With 23 people, there is about a 50.7% chance that two share a birthday, because 23 people make 253 pairs.
In cryptography
With N possible values, a collision is expected after roughly √N samples. A 64-bit block repeats after about 2³² blocks, the basis of the Sweet32 attack on 3DES.
Hashes
A 256-bit hash has about 128 bits of collision resistance.
example: The calculation
The chance of no match among 23 people is (365/365)(364/365)…(343/365) ≈ 0.493, so the chance of a match is about 0.507.

title: Perfect secrecy
lead: Why the one-time pad cannot be broken, and why it is rarely used.
sections: The proof

If the key is uniformly random, as long as the message and used once, then every plaintext of that length is equally consistent with a ciphertext. The ciphertext tells an attacker nothing beyond length.
The cost
Shannon showed that perfect secrecy needs at least as much key as message.
When it fails
Reuse cancels the key: (P₁ ⊕ K) ⊕ (P₂ ⊕ K) = P₁ ⊕ P₂. That is how Project Venona read Soviet messages.
example: A single letter
Ciphertext X could be any letter. With key letter C it decrypts to one letter, with key letter D to another. All 26 keys are equally likely, so all 26 plaintexts are equally likely.
